Subject: Stepping back from the poster job

Dear Seema,

I owe you an honest note. This week I have two graded assignments, the lab file and the club fest, all before Saturday. Last night I wrote them in a row with the date and the marks beside each. The assignments count for marks and cannot move. The lab file is due Thursday morning and is worth the most. The fest posters are not due till next week, and I realise someone else can do them. If I keep all four, all four will be done badly. So I have to let the posters go.

I am sorry to drop this at short notice. I will pass on my sketches tonight and help with hanging them if I can.

Deepika

qa.q: Which day is the lab file due?
qa.a: The lab file is due Thursday morning.

qa.q: What did Deepika think when writing the tasks in a row with dates and marks?
qa.a: Deepika felt uneasy and a little guilty, realising that all four tasks could not be done well, so the least valuable one, the posters, had to be dropped.

qa.q: What other approach could Deepika try before dropping the posters, and why?
qa.a: Deepika could ask Seema to split the poster work in two, since sharing the job might keep it alive without hurting the marks.

qa.q: How might Seema see the note arriving at short notice?
qa.a: Seema may feel worried about finding a new helper, but honest words and a promise of the sketches make it easier to plan around.

grounding: A student facing heavy deadlines sorts tasks by due date and marks and drops the least valuable item.

Leela, you asked how I survived week nine. This is Ankita, and here's the answer: I dropped something, on purpose.
That week I had the circuits assignment due Wednesday, worth ten marks. The economics essay due Friday, worth twenty. The lab file for Thursday's viva, which you can't sit without. And I'd promised to design posters for the dance club's event on Saturday.
On Monday night I wrote all four on a sheet with two numbers beside each: days left, marks at stake. The lab file had no marks of its own, but no file meant no viva, so it went first. The essay was worth the most. Circuits was due soonest but worth the least of the three.
The posters had zero marks and a whole club depending on them, so I didn't just vanish. I called Mitali, who's good at design, and asked her to take them. That freed Friday night.
I finished all three academic things. Mitali's posters were better than mine would have been.

qa.q: How many marks was the economics essay worth?
How did Ankita feel about dropping the posters, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ankita felt a bit guilty about the club depending on the posters, which is why Ankita didn't just vanish but asked Mitali to take them.

qa.q: What else could Ankita have done if Mitali had said no?
qa.a: Tell the club early and offer a simpler poster or a later date, rather than squeezing it in and risking the assignments.

qa.q: How might Mitali see being asked to take the posters?
qa.a: Mitali may feel trusted and pleased to help, and the club gets better posters.

grounding: Shows a student sorting two assignments, a lab file and a club task by deadline and marks, and handing off the least valuable one.

I'm Jyoti, Ayesha's roommate, and on Sunday night I watched her do something odd with a pile of sticky notes.
She had five of them on the wall: 'Stats assignment – Tue – 15 marks', 'Chem lab file – Thu – needed for viva', 'History essay – Fri – 25 marks', 'Quiz prep – Fri – 5 marks', and 'Hackathon – Sat – 0 marks, just for fun'.
She stood there muttering. 'Lab file first, no file no viva. Essay next, most marks. Stats is due first, so tomorrow night.' Then she held the quiz one for a long time. 'Five marks. I'll revise on the bus.'
The hackathon note she took down and stuck on her cupboard door. 'Next month's one,' she said. She messaged her team that she was out this time.
I don't know if she was sad about it. But by Friday night all four notes were in the bin, and she slept nine hours.

qa.q: Which note did Ayesha stick on her cupboard door?
How might Ayesha have felt taking down the hackathon note?
qa.a: She may have felt a little disappointed to miss something fun, but calm and clear that the marked work mattered more this week.

qa.q: What could Ayesha do to make next month's hackathon possible?
qa.a: Check that month's deadlines early and keep the weekend free, so the fun event does not clash again.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's hackathon team feel about her message?
qa.a: They may be disappointed but grateful for the early notice, which gives them time to find someone else.

grounding: Shows a student sorting tasks by deadline and marks, revising lightly for a small quiz and dropping a no-mark hackathon in a heavy week.
